concepts.label: Sorrieu's Vision of Democratic and Social Republics
concepts.cardText: In 1848 Frédéric Sorrieu, a French artist, prepared a series of four prints visualising his dream of a world made up of democratic and social Republics. The German flag in the print expressed liberal hopes in 1848 to unify the German-speaking principalities into a nation-state under a democratic constitution, although the German peoples did not yet exist as a united nation.

concepts.topicTitle: Introduction: the idea of the nation
concepts.label: Nationalism and the Nation-State in Nineteenth-Century Europe
concepts.cardText: During the nineteenth century, nationalism emerged as a force which brought about sweeping changes in the political and mental world of Europe. The end result was the emergence of the nation-state in place of the multi-national dynastic empires of Europe. A nation-state was one in which the majority of citizens, and not only its rulers, came to develop a sense of common identity and shared history or descent. This commonness did not exist from time immemorial; it was forged through struggles, through the actions of leaders and the common people.

concepts.topicTitle: Introduction: the idea of the nation
concepts.label: Ernst Renan's Idea of a Nation
concepts.cardText: In a lecture at the Sorbonne in 1882, the French philosopher Ernst Renan criticised the notion that a nation is formed by a common language, race, religion or territory. He said a nation is the culmination of a long past of endeavours, sacrifice and devotion; common glories in the past, a common will in the present, great deeds performed together and the wish to perform still more are the essential conditions of being a people. A nation is a large-scale solidarity whose existence is a daily plebiscite, and the existence of nations is a guarantee of liberty.

concepts.topicTitle: The French Revolution and the idea of the nation
concepts.label: The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation
concepts.cardText: The first clear expression of nationalism came with the French Revolution in 1789. The changes that followed led to the transfer of sovereignty from the monarchy to a body of French citizens, and the revolution proclaimed that it was the people who would henceforth constitute the nation and shape its destiny. To create a sense of collective identity, the revolutionaries introduced la patrie and le citoyen, a new tricolour flag, the National Assembly, new hymns and oaths, a centralised administration with uniform laws, abolition of internal customs duties, a uniform system of weights and measures, and French as the common language of the nation.

concepts.topicTitle: The French Revolution and the idea of the nation
concepts.label: Napoleon's Administrative Reforms and Their Mixed Reception
concepts.cardText: Napoleon destroyed democracy in France by returning to monarchy, but in the administrative field he incorporated revolutionary principles to make the system more rational and efficient. The Civil Code of 1804, the Napoleonic Code, did away with privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property, and it was exported to the regions under French control. In the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, Italy and Germany he simplified administrative divisions, abolished the feudal system, freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues, removed guild restrictions and improved transport and communication. Businessmen welcomed uniform laws, weights, measures and a common currency. Yet the initial welcome turned to hostility because the new arrangements did not go hand in hand with political freedom, and increased taxation, censorship and forced conscription outweighed the advantages.

concepts.topicTitle: The making of nationalism in Europe
concepts.label: Europe Before Nation-States: The Habsburg Empire
concepts.cardText: In the mid-eighteenth century there were no nation-states as we know them today. What is now Germany, Italy and Switzerland were divided into kingdoms, duchies and cantons whose rulers had their autonomous territories. Eastern and Central Europe were under autocratic monarchies in which lived diverse peoples who did not see themselves as sharing a collective identity or common culture. The Habsburg Empire that ruled Austria-Hungary was a patchwork of many different regions and peoples, and the only tie binding the diverse groups together was a common allegiance to the emperor.

concepts.topicTitle: The making of nationalism in Europe
concepts.label: The Aristocracy and the New Middle Class
concepts.cardText: Socially and politically, a landed aristocracy was the dominant class on the continent. They owned estates in the countryside and town-houses and spoke French for diplomacy and in high society. This powerful aristocracy was numerically a small group; the majority of the population was the peasantry. In Western and parts of Central Europe the growth of industrial production and trade meant the growth of towns and commercial classes producing for the market. Industrialisation began in England in the second half of the eighteenth century, but in France and parts of the German states only during the nineteenth. New social groups came into being: a working-class population and middle classes of industrialists, businessmen and professionals. Ideas of national unity following the abolition of aristocratic privileges gained popularity among the educated, liberal middle classes.

concepts.topicTitle: The making of nationalism in Europe
concepts.label: What Did Liberal Nationalism Stand For?
concepts.cardText: Ideas of national unity in early-nineteenth-century Europe were closely allied to the ideology of liberalism, from the Latin root liber, meaning free. For the new middle classes liberalism stood for freedom for the individual and equality of all before the law, and politically for government by consent, an end to autocracy and clerical privileges, a constitution and representative government through parliament. Liberals also stressed the inviolability of private property. Equality before the law did not mean universal suffrage: in revolutionary France only property-owning men could vote, and the Napoleonic Code reduced women to the status of a minor. In the economic sphere, liberalism stood for the freedom of markets and the abolition of state-imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital.

concepts.topicTitle: The making of nationalism in Europe
concepts.label: The Zollverein and Economic Nationalism
concepts.cardText: In the German-speaking regions, Napoleon's measures had created a confederation of 39 states, each with its own currency, weights and measures. A merchant travelling in 1833 from Hamburg to Nuremberg had to pass through 11 customs barriers and pay a customs duty of about 5 per cent at each. The new commercial classes saw such conditions as obstacles to economic exchange and growth and argued for a unified economic territory. In 1834 a customs union, the zollverein, was formed at the initiative of Prussia and joined by most German states. It abolished tariff barriers and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two. A network of railways further stimulated mobility, harnessing economic interests to national unification, and a wave of economic nationalism strengthened the wider nationalist sentiment.

concepts.topicTitle: The making of nationalism in Europe
concepts.label: A New Conservatism after 1815: The Treaty of Vienna
concepts.cardText: Following the defeat of Napoleon in 1815, European governments were driven by conservatism: the belief that established, traditional institutions like the monarchy, the Church, social hierarchies, property and the family should be preserved. Conservatives realised from Napoleon's changes that modernisation could strengthen the monarchy, through a modern army, an efficient bureaucracy and a dynamic economy. In 1815 Britain, Russia, Prussia and Austria met at Vienna, hosted by Duke Metternich, and drew up the Treaty of Vienna to undo most of the changes of the Napoleonic wars. The Bourbon dynasty was restored, France lost annexed territories, states were set up on its boundaries to prevent French expansion, and the main intention was to restore the overthrown monarchies and create a new conservative order. Conservative regimes were autocratic, did not tolerate dissent, and imposed censorship, though freedom of the press became a major liberal-nationalist issue.

concepts.topicTitle: The making of nationalism in Europe
concepts.label: The Revolutionaries and Giuseppe Mazzini
concepts.cardText: During the years following 1815, the fear of repression drove many liberal-nationalists underground. Secret societies sprang up in many European states to train revolutionaries and spread their ideas. To be revolutionary meant a commitment to oppose monarchical forms established after the Vienna Congress and to fight for liberty and freedom, and most revolutionaries saw the creation of nation-states as a necessary part of this struggle. The Italian revolutionary Giuseppe Mazzini, born in Genoa in 1805, joined the Carbonari, was exiled in 1831, and founded Young Italy in Marseilles and Young Europe in Berne. He believed God had intended nations to be the natural units of mankind, so Italy had to be forged into a single unified republic within a wider alliance of nations. Metternich called him the most dangerous enemy of the social order.

concepts.label: The Romantic Imagination and National Feeling
concepts.cardText: Culture played an important role in creating the idea of the nation: art and poetry, stories and music helped express and shape nationalist feelings. concepts.label: Language, Poland and the Grimm Brothers
concepts.cardText: The emphasis on vernacular language and the collection of local folklore was not just to recover an ancient national spirit, but also to carry the modern nationalist message to large audiences who were mostly illiterate. Poland had been partitioned at the end of the eighteenth century by Russia, Prussia and Austria, yet national feelings were kept alive through music and language. Karol Kurpinski turned folk dances like the polonaise and mazurka into nationalist symbols. After Russian occupation, Polish was forced out of schools, and after the crushed rebellion of 1831 many clergy used Polish as a weapon of national resistance; the use of Polish became a symbol of the struggle against Russian dominance. The Grimm brothers collected German folktales, believing them expressions of a pure and authentic German spirit, as part of the effort to oppose French domination and create a German national identity.

concepts.topicTitle: The age of revolutions: 1830-1848
concepts.label: Hunger, Hardship and Popular Revolt
concepts.cardText: The 1830s were years of great economic hardship in Europe. Population grew enormously, there were more job seekers than jobs, and people migrated to overcrowded city slums. Small producers faced stiff competition from cheap machine-made goods imported from England. In regions where the aristocracy still enjoyed power, peasants struggled under feudal dues and obligations, and a rise in food prices or a bad harvest led to widespread pauperism. In 1848 food shortages and unemployment brought the people of Paris onto the roads; barricades were erected, Louis Philippe fled, and the National Assembly proclaimed a Republic, granted suffrage to all adult males above 21, guaranteed the right to work and set up national workshops. Earlier, in 1845, weavers in Silesia revolted against contractors who drastically reduced their payments.

concepts.topicTitle: The age of revolutions: 1830-1848
concepts.label: 1848: The Revolution of the Liberals
concepts.cardText: Parallel to the revolts of the poor in 1848, a revolution led by the educated middle classes was under way. In February 1848 the monarch abdicated in France and a republic based on universal male suffrage was proclaimed. Where nation-states did not yet exist, such as Germany, Italy, Poland and the Austro-Hungarian Empire, liberal middle-class men and women combined their demands for constitutionalism with national unification: a constitution, freedom of the press and freedom of association. In Frankfurt, on 18 May 1848, 831 elected representatives drafted a constitution for a German nation headed by a monarchy subject to a parliament. When they offered the crown to Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia he rejected it and joined other monarchs to oppose the assembly. The parliament, dominated by the middle classes, resisted the demands of workers and artisans and lost their support, and troops forced the assembly to disband.

concepts.topicTitle: The making of Germany and Italy; Britain
concepts.label: Germany: Can the Army Be the Architect of a Nation?
concepts.cardText: After 1848, nationalism in Europe moved away from its association with democracy and revolution, and conservatives often mobilised nationalist sentiment to promote state power and political domination. From then on Prussia took the lead in national unification. Its chief minister Otto von Bismarck was the architect of the process, carried out with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy. Three wars over seven years, with Austria, Denmark and France, ended in Prussian victory and completed unification. In January 1871 the Prussian king William I was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles, and the new state emphasised modernising the currency, banking, legal and judicial systems.

concepts.topicTitle: The making of Germany and Italy; Britain
concepts.label: Italy Unified
concepts.cardText: Like Germany, Italy had a long history of political fragmentation. In the mid-nineteenth century Italy was divided into seven states, of which only Sardinia-Piedmont was ruled by an Italian princely house; the north was under the Austrian Habsburgs, the centre under the Pope and the south under the Bourbon kings of Spain. Mazzini's uprisings failed in 1831 and 1848, so the mantle fell on Sardinia-Piedmont under King Victor Emmanuel II. Chief Minister Cavour, neither a revolutionary nor a democrat, engineered a diplomatic alliance with France, and Sardinia-Piedmont defeated the Austrian forces in 1859. Giuseppe Garibaldi led armed volunteers into South Italy in 1860, won the support of local peasants and drove out the Spanish rulers. In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy, and the Papal States joined in 1870 when France withdrew its troops from Rome.

concepts.topicTitle: The making of Germany and Italy; Britain
concepts.label: The Strange Case of Britain
concepts.cardText: The formation of the nation-state in Britain was not the result of a sudden upheaval or revolution but of a long-drawn-out process. There was no British nation prior to the eighteenth century; the primary identities of people in the British Isles were ethnic ones, such as English, Welsh, Scot or Irish. As the English nation grew in wealth, importance and power, it extended its influence over the others. The English parliament, which had seized power from the monarchy in 1688, was the instrument through which the nation-state with England at its centre was forged. The Act of Union (1707) between England and Scotland meant England could impose its influence on Scotland, whose culture and institutions were suppressed; Highlanders were forbidden their Gaelic language and national dress. After the failed revolt of Wolfe Tone and his United Irishmen in 1798, Ireland was forcibly incorporated into the United Kingdom in 1801. A new British nation was forged by promoting English culture, with the older nations surviving as subordinate partners.

concepts.topicTitle: Visualising the nation; nationalism and imperialism
concepts.label: Visualising the Nation: Marianne and Germania
concepts.cardText: Artists in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries gave a face to a nation by personifying it, representing a country as if it were a person, usually a female figure. The figure did not stand for any real woman; it gave the abstract idea of the nation a concrete form, becoming an allegory of the nation. In France the female allegory was christened Marianne, a popular Christian name that underlined the idea of a people's nation; her characteristics were drawn from Liberty and the Republic: the red cap, the tricolour and the cockade. Statues of Marianne were erected in public squares, and her image was marked on coins and stamps. Germania became the allegory of the German nation and wears a crown of oak leaves, as the German oak stands for heroism.

concepts.topicTitle: Visualising the nation; nationalism and imperialism
concepts.label: Nationalism and Imperialism: The Balkans
concepts.cardText: By the last quarter of the nineteenth century nationalism no longer retained its idealistic liberal-democratic sentiment of the first half of the century, but became a narrow creed with limited ends. Nationalist groups became increasingly intolerant of each other and ever ready to go to war, and the major European powers manipulated the nationalist aspirations of subject peoples to further their own imperialist aims. The most serious source of nationalist tension after 1871 was the Balkans, a region of geographical and ethnic variation whose inhabitants were broadly known as Slavs, with a large part under the Ottoman Empire. Romantic nationalism and the disintegration of the Ottoman Empire made it explosive. The Balkan states were fiercely jealous of each other, each hoping to gain territory at the expense of the others, and big power rivalry over trade, colonies and naval and military might added to the conflict, leading to a series of wars and finally the First World War.

concepts.topicTitle: Visualising the nation; nationalism and imperialism
concepts.label: Anti-Imperial Nationalism Outside Europe
concepts.cardText: Nationalism, aligned with imperialism, led Europe to disaster in 1914. Meanwhile, many countries colonised by European powers in the nineteenth century began to oppose imperial domination. The anti-imperial movements were nationalist in the sense that they struggled to form independent nation-states and were inspired by a sense of collective national unity, forged in confrontation with imperialism. European ideas of nationalism were nowhere replicated, for people everywhere developed their own specific variety of nationalism, but the idea that societies should be organised into nation-states came to be accepted as natural and universal.
